qs.q: In which CHD does the right ventricle inflow tract function haemodynamically as an atrial chamber?
qs.e: Apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet causes atrialization of the RV inflow tract — it receives atrial pressure and contracts out of synchrony with the functional RV.

qs.q: Which congenital heart defect is characterised by absence of a direct connection between the right atrium and right ventricle?
qs.e: There is no tricuspid valve orifice connecting RA to RV. Survival depends on an ASD for right-sided drainage and a VSD or PDA for pulmonary blood flow.

ai.title: Right Ventricular Pathology and Dysfunction
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: The right ventricle is a thin-walled, compliant chamber uniquely sensitive to afterload changes and dependent on preload. Pathology arises from left-sided heart disease, pulmonary vascular disorders, intrinsic infarction, or cardiomyopathy, presenting as systemic venous congestion.

sections.p: Right ventricular (RV) pathology encompasses structural, ischaemic, or functional failure of the right ventricle to pump venous return through the pulmonary circulation at normal central venous pressures. Diagnosis is clinical and echocardiographic.
b: Crescent-shaped chamber with a thin free wall adapted to low pulmonary vascular resistance.
Cannot tolerate acute rises in afterload, which trigger rapid dilatation and contractile failure.
Diagnosis rests on signs of systemic congestion plus objective evidence of RV enlargement or dysfunction.

sections.p: Staging follows functional impairment and the degree of hemodynamic collapse.
b: Compensated RV strain: Elevated RV systolic pressure without overt clinical congestion.
Decompensated RV failure: Systemic venous congestion with peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly, and elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP).
Cardiogenic shock from RV failure: Hypotension, oliguria, and cool peripheries due to reduced left ventricular filling from ventricular interdependence.

sections.p: Pathology is predominantly secondary to left-sided heart disease, followed by pulmonary vascular and intrinsic RV diseases.
b: Left heart failure: Secondary pulmonary venous hypertension from rheumatic heart disease, dilated cardiomyopathy, or hypertensive heart disease.
Pulmonary parenchymal and vascular disease: Cor pulmonale from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, post-tuberculosis fibrosis, or pulmonary schistosomiasis.
Right ventricular myocardial infarction: Typically caused by right coronary artery occlusion in inferior wall infarcts.
Infective endocarditis: Tricuspid valve involvement in intravenous drug use or septic thrombophlebitis.
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy: Fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium predisposing to ventricular arrhythmias.

sections.p: Bedside examination demonstrates systemic venous congestion alongside pulmonary hypertension signs, often without pulmonary crackles.
b: Elevated JVP, often with prominent 'v' waves if tricuspid regurgitation is present.
Pulsatile, tender hepatomegaly and ascites with shifting dullness.
Bilateral pitting pedal oedema extending proximally up the lower limbs.
Left parasternal heave signifying right ventricular hypertrophy or enlargement.
Accentuated pulmonary component of the second heart sound (loud P2) and pansystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation.

t.b: Identifies right ventricular strain or infarction; right-sided leads (V4R) confirm RV involvement during acute inferior myocardial infarction.
Assesses RV size, tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, and pulmonary artery systolic pressure; distinguishes pure RV disease from secondary left-sided failure.
Answers if RV is dilated when formal echo is unavailable; evaluates inferior vena cava plethora and lack of respiratory collapse.
Detects cardiomegaly and pulmonary disease; the RV is anterior so it does not form a lateral heart border on PA film.
Quantifies myocardial necrosis and ventricular wall stress; BNP confirms ventricular strain even if echocardiography is delayed.

sections.p: Recognising early hemodynamic collapse prevents fatal outcomes.
b: Profound hypotension following nitrates or diuretics due to extreme preload sensitivity.
Ventricular interdependence: Dilated RV shifts the interventricular septum leftward, restricting left ventricular filling and dropping cardiac output.
Malignant ventricular arrhythmias triggered by fibrofatty infiltration or ischaemia.
Hepatosplenomegaly progressing to hepatic congestion and acute coagulopathy.

sections.p: Prioritise hemodynamic stability by maintaining adequate preload while avoiding volume overload; target the underlying driver.
b: Optimise preload: Judicious intravenous normal saline challenges in isolated RV infarction; avoid overfilling which worsens septal shift.
Careful decongestion: Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) for systemic congestion; avoid overdiuresis to prevent precipitous drops in stroke volume.
Inotropic support: Dobutamine or adrenaline to restore RV contractility and maintain systemic perfusion pressure.
Afterload reduction: Oxygen to reverse hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction; specific pulmonary vasodilators only for confirmed pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Avoid vasodilators: Nitrates and ACE inhibitors are strictly avoided in acute RV strain/infarction due to fatal preload collapse.

sections.p: Long-term monitoring centres on treating the primary respiratory or valvular etiology.
b: Secondary prevention of rheumatic heart disease with regular intramuscular benzathine penicillin.
Early diagnosis and treatment of tuberculosis and schistosomiasis to halt irreversible pulmonary fibrosis and vascular remodeling.
Periodic assessment of jugular venous pressure, weight changes, and renal function on diuretics.

sections.p: Differentiating isolated RV failure from conditions mimicking systemic congestion is essential for proper management.
b: Constrictive pericarditis: Presents with elevated JVP and ascites, but characterized by pericardial knock and calcification without primary RV dilatation.
Liver cirrhosis: Features ascites and peripheral oedema, but JVP is completely flat or normal.
Severe bilateral deep vein thrombosis: Lower limb swelling without raised JVP or hepatomegaly.
Nephrotic syndrome: Severe generalized oedema with normal JVP, proteinuria, and preserved RV anatomy.

sections.p: Pitfalls in investigation interpretation can cause misdiagnosis.
b: PA chest radiograph: Severe RV enlargement may push the left ventricle posterolaterally, giving a false appearance of left ventricular enlargement.
Serum transaminases: High elevation from passive hepatic congestion ('shock liver') can be misattributed to acute viral or toxic hepatitis.
Electrocardiogram in cor pulmonale: Chronic RV hypertrophy can cause poor R-wave progression in anterior leads, mimicking anterior myocardial infarction.

whenToSeekHelp: Systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg with signs of peripheral hypoperfusion
Syncope or pre-syncope in a patient with suspected pulmonary hypertension
Rapidly rising jugular venous pressure accompanied by severe oliguria
Sudden worsening of dyspnoea with new right-sided chest pain

faq.q: Why does the right ventricle not form a heart border on a normal PA chest X-ray?
faq.a: The right ventricle is an anterior structure lying directly behind the sternum; the right border is formed by the right atrium and the left border by the left ventricle.

faq.q: Why are nitrates contraindicated in acute right ventricular myocardial infarction?
faq.a: The ischaemic right ventricle is extraordinarily preload-dependent; nitrates induce venous dilation and drop preload, causing sudden cardiac output collapse and shock.

faq.q: What is the mechanism of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC)?
faq.a: Mutations in desmosomal proteins cause progressive myocyte detachment and apoptosis, leading to fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium and re-entrant ventricular tachycardias.

exam: A patient with an inferior STEMI develops severe hypotension after one sublingual nitrate. What happened and what is the immediate management? — Nitrate venodilation caused severe RV preload reduction in concomitant RV infarction; manage by immediately stopping nitrates, elevating legs, and giving an intravenous fluid challenge.

Why does a heavily dilated right ventricle cause a drop in left ventricular stroke volume? — Ventricular interdependence: the thin-walled RV dilates against the shared pericardial space, shifting the interventricular septum into the LV cavity, impairing LV diastolic filling.

On a PA chest radiograph, which cardiac chamber forms the left cardiac border, and how does RV enlargement alter this? — The left ventricle forms the border; massive RV enlargement rotates the heart posteriorly and leftward, displacing the LV and mimicking LV cardiomegaly.

A young patient presents with ascites and raised JVP. How do you distinguish RV failure from constrictive pericarditis at the bedside? — Look for Kussmaul sign and a pericardial knock in constrictive pericarditis; a loud P2, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, or parasternal heave favours RV failure.

How does untreated pulmonary schistosomiasis cause RV failure? — Schistosoma eggs embolize to pulmonary arterioles, inciting granulomatous inflammation, vascular remodeling, obliteration of the pulmonary vascular bed, and severe pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Why must diuretics be used with extreme caution in pure cor pulmonale? — The right ventricle relies on a high filling pressure to overcome elevated pulmonary vascular resistance; excessive diuresis drops preload and precipitates circulatory collapse.

What specific lead should you request on an ECG if you suspect right ventricular involvement, and what is diagnostic? — Request right-sided lead V4R; ST-segment elevation of 1 mm or more in V4R confirms acute RV infarction.
